rv.q: Things bog down after intermission, when there are one too many earnest speeches and saintly Rita admits to an unease with her marriage.
The only problem with Casa Valentina is a rather big one: Fierstein sets up 80 percent of his story, then doesn’t know how to finish it for maximum impact.
For its first half-hour or so, when 'Casa Valentina' is more show than tell, it promises to be Mr. Fierstein's most engagingly insightful play to date.
Having set up these wonderful characters, Fierstein stumbles dramaturgically once the conflict is introduced, as if he’s unsure where to go from there.
Along the way, bless him, he understands how to entertain.
In any case, the way these motives come together, or don’t, to advance the cause of liberation for “self-made women” is the subject of this fascinating if somewhat musty play.
But the plot is messy, the action static, and attempts to probe the psychosexual dynamic of transvestism are tentative and superficial.

Fierstein's compassion for his characters never flags, and director Joe Mantello juggles the vivacious and bleak elements of the play — its warmth and wryness, both characteristic of the playwright — adroitly.
His fact-inspired story -- directed with sensitivity and style by Joe Mantello -- unfolds at a Catskills bungalow colony that caters to heterosexual transvestites.
Fierstein’s meticulous dialogue, Joe Mantello’s smooth and confident direction, the cast’s flawless performances.
That he hasn't hardly detracts from an amazing accomplishment and one that, as the Tony season ends, will be a strong contender for the coveted prize.
But its illumination of a neglected corner of human activity is diverting, and often thought-provoking.
With “Casa Valentina,” those victims are looking more pathetic than sympathetic.

There is some rich characterization and even insight here, but Casa is too much like a social and political debate rather than an honest depiction of stigmatized people attempting to find solace and comfort with each other.
Her inclusion in the cast lineup and Cullum’s exceptional performance add a layer of authenticity that lingers long after the curtain falls.

cn.t: Fierstein's fact-inspired drama about 1960s heterosexual cross-dressers draws praise for its sensitive direction and strong ensemble, but critics find the play more notable for its intentions than its insights, with too much talk undermining quieter moments.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
